text.p: Sterling bounced back from early lows here after a robust UK Purchasing Managers Index (PMI) further dampened any lingering talk of pre-election UK interest rate cuts, analysts said.

The pound retreated in early trade after setting a 20-month peak at 2.3905 late Monday but key support at the July high at 2.3820 held fast. Its bounce was helped by the impressive details of the puchasing managers report, traders said.
The September UK PMI rose to 53.4, its highest level in 17 months, from a revised August index at 52.0. It was the biggest monthly rise in output and new orders since autumn 1994.
The purchasing managers' prices index, although still below the break-even 50 level, rose to 44.0 from 41.7.
"The September PMI was a very strong survey, and looks to be the final nail in the coffin of rate cut hopes," said Lee Ferridge, treasury economist at NatWest Markets.
"I think sterling can probably get back above 2.40, but a lot of the move is dependent on dollar/mark and I'd be nervous about the pound at those levels," said Ferridge.
The PMI report comes in the wake of news on Monday that September M0 money supply grew 7.0 percent year-on-year and new consumer credit was up 997 million pounds in August.
At 1035 GMT, the pound was trading at 2.3848/53 little changed from 2.3848/55 late Monday. Against the dollar, it was at $1.5652/59 compared with $1.5650/60 late yesterday.

Traders said that while sterling/mark may struggle at 2.40 for now, cable should rise a little further near-term to at least the $1.5725 area. That is a 50 percent retracement of the its decline through 1994 and 1995.

"Sterling/mark's rise has steadied following the pause in the dollar's rise seen yesterday," said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered. "With the dollar perhaps now entering a corrective phase, cable looks placed to benefit."
Traders will keep an eye on the UK opposition Labour Party's annual conference, meantime, with Labour leader Tony Blair due to give his keynote speech later this afternoon.
Of key interest will be Labour's stance on Europe and possible UK participation in monetary union.

Labour foreign affairs spokesman Robin Cook said earlier today Labour sees the advantages of a single currency but that a decision on whether or not to join the first wave would not have to be made for another year yet. The latest opinion poll put Labour 27 points clear of the ruling Conservatives.
